Notable geological formations in the territory include the *Canberra Formation*, the *Pittman Formation*, *Black Mountain Sandstone* and *State Circle Shale*.

In the 1840s [fossils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil) of [brachiopods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brachiopod) and [trilobites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trilobite) from the [Silurian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silurian) period were discovered at Woolshed Creek near [Duntroon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duntroon,_Australian_Capital_Territory). At the time, these were the oldest fossils discovered in Australia, though this record has now been far surpassed.<sup>[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-61)</sup> Other specific geological places of interest include the State Circle cutting and the Deakin [anticline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anticline).[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-62)[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-63)

The oldest rocks in the territory date from the [Ordovician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordovician) around 480 million years ago. During this period the region along with most of Eastern Australia was part of the ocean floor; formations from this period include the *Black Mountain Sandstone* formation and the *Pittman Formation* consisting largely of [quartz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartz)-rich [sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandstone), [siltstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siltstone) and [shale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shale). These formations became exposed when the ocean floor was raised by a major [volcanic activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orogeny) in the [Devonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devonian) forming much of the east coast of Australia.

The environments range from [alpine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_climate) area on the higher mountains, to [sclerophyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sclerophyll) forest and to [woodland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodland). Much of the territory has been cleared for grazing and is also burnt off by [bushfires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bushfires_in_Australia) several times per century. The kinds of plants can be grouped into [vascular plants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vascular_plants), that include [gymnosperms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymnosperm), flowering plants, and [ferns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fern), as well as [bryophytes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryophyte), [lichens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lichen), fungi and freshwater [algae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algae). Four flowering plants are endemic to the territory. Several lichens are unique to the territory. Most plants in the territory are characteristic of the [Flora of Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_flora) and include well known plants such as [Grevillea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grevillea), [Eucalyptus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eucalyptus) trees and [kangaroo grass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangaroo_grass).

The native forest in the territory was almost wholly [eucalypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eucalyptus) species and provided a resource for fuel and domestic purposes. By the early 1960s, logging had depleted the eucalypt, and concern about water quality led to the forests being closed. Interest in forestry began in 1915 with trials of a number of species including *[Pinus radiata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinus_radiata)* on the slopes of Mount Stromlo. Since then, plantations have been expanded, with the benefit of reducing erosion in the Cotter catchment, and the forests are also popular recreation areas.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-64)

Fauna in the territory includes representatives from most major [Australian animal groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauna_of_Australia). This includes kangaroos, wallabies, koalas, platypus, echidna, emu, kookaburras and dragon lizards.

Unlike the states of Australia which have their own constitutions, territories are governed under a Commonwealth statute<sup>[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-:10-65)</sup>—for the ACT, the *[Australian Capital Territory (Self-Government) Act 1988](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Capital_Territory_(Self-Government)_Act_1988>)*.<sup>[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-66)</sup> The *Self-Government Act* constitutes a democratic government for the territory consisting of a popularly elected [Legislative Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Capital_Territory_Legislative_Assembly) which elects a [Chief Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Minister_of_the_Australian_Capital_Territory) from among its membership who, in turn, appoints an Executive consisting of a number of Ministers.

The executive power of the territory rests with the [ACT government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_Australian_Capital_Territory), headed by the Chief Minister (currently the [Labor Party](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Labor_Party_(Australian_Capital_Territory_Branch)>)'s [Andrew Barr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Barr)) and consists of ministers appointed by them. The ministers are supported by the ACT Public Service, which is arranged into directorates, and a number of public authorities.<sup>[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-67)</sup> The Chief Minister is the equivalent of a [State Premier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiers_and_chief_ministers_of_the_Australian_states_and_territories) and sits on the National Cabinet.<sup>[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-68)</sup> Unlike the states, there is no [vice-regal representative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governors_of_the_Australian_states) who chairs the executive government council. The Chief Minister performs many of the roles that a state governor normally holds in the context of a state; however, the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly gazettes the laws and summons meetings of the Assembly.

The [ACT Labor party](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Labor_Party_(Australian_Capital_Territory_Branch)>) has been in power since 2001.

The legislative power of the territory is vested in the unicameral [Legislative Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Capital_Territory_Legislative_Assembly).  The assembly has 25 [members](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Current_members_of_the_Australian_Capital_Territory_Legislative_Assembly), elected from [five electorates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electorates_of_the_Australian_Capital_Territory) using the [Hare-Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hare–Clark_electoral_system) single transferable voting system.<sup>[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-69)</sup> The assembly is presided over by the Speaker (currently the Liberal Party's [Jeremy Hanson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Hanson)). The Assembly has almost all of the same powers as the state parliaments, the power to "make laws for the peace, order, and good government of the Territory", with limited exceptions relating to the territory's unique relationship with the commonwealth.<sup>[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-70)</sup> The Hare-Clark voting system was adopted after [a referendum in 1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_Australian_Capital_Territory_electoral_system_referendum) and was entrenched by another referendum in 1995.<sup>[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-71)</sup> The electoral system cannot be changed except by a two-thirds majority in the Assembly or a majority vote of support at a public referendum.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-72)

There is no level of [local government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_government_in_Australia) below the territory government as in the states and the functions associated with local government are carried out principally by the [Transport Canberra and City Services Directorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_Canberra_&_City_Services).<sup>[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-73)</sup> There is an indigenous voice to the ACT government, called the [Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Elected Body](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aboriginal_and_Torres_Strait_Islander_Elected_Body).[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-74)

Despite the wide powers of the territory government, the federal government continues to have power over the territory. This includes an unused power to dissolve the assembly and appoint a caretaker government in extraordinary circumstances.<sup>[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-75)</sup> The federal and territory governments share some officers, such as the [Ombudsman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Ombudsman).<sup>[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-76)</sup> The federal parliament also retains the power to make any law for the territory under [section 122 of the Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Section_122_of_the_Constitution_of_Australia) and an exclusive power to legislate for the "seat of government".[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-:10-65)<sup>[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-77)</sup> Territory laws which conflict with federal law are inoperable to the extent of the inconsistency.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-78)<sup>[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-79)</sup> Land in the territory that is designated to be "National Land" under federal law remains under the control of the federal government, usually represented by the [National Capital Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Capital_Authority).<sup>[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-80)</sup> The federal parliament can disallow laws enacted by the Assembly by a joint resolution of both houses of Parliament, a power which replaced a federal executive veto in 2011.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-81)[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-vetopower-82)

The judicial power of the territory is exercised by the territory courts. These are the [Supreme Court of the Australian Capital Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_Australian_Capital_Territory), the [Magistrates Court of the Australian Capital Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magistrates_Court_of_the_Australian_Capital_Territory) (with summary jurisdiction), and the [ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACT_Civil_and_Administrative_Tribunal). From 2001, appeals from the Supreme Court are heard by a panel of Supreme Court judges sitting as the Court of Appeal.<sup>[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-83)</sup> The current Chief Justice is [Lucy McCallum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucy_McCallum) and the current Chief Magistrate is [Lorraine Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorraine_Walker).

The [Federal Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Court_of_Australia) has concurrent jurisdiction over civil matters arising under territory law, a fact which has become increasingly important to the practice of [defamation law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defamation) across Australia.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-84)[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-85)[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-86)

Policing services are provided by the [ACT Policing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ACT_Policing) unit of the [Australian Federal Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Federal_Police) under agreements between the territory government, the federal government, and the police force.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-87)[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-88)[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-89)[Canberra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canberra) had the lowest rate of crime of any capital city in Australia as of February 2019[\[update\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Australian_Capital_Territory&action=edit)[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-90)

In the Australian [federal parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Australia), the territory is represented by three members of the [House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_House_of_Representatives), for the [Division of Bean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_of_Bean), the [Division of Canberra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_of_Canberra) and the [Division of Fenner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_of_Fenner) and two [Senators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Senate). The member for Bean also represents voters of [Norfolk Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norfolk_Island) while the member for Fenner also represent voters of the [Jervis Bay Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jervis_Bay_Territory).

The [continent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continent) of **Australia**, sometimes known in technical contexts as **Sahul** ([//](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English), [*sə-HOOL*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key)),[\[note 5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-5)**Australia-New Guinea**, **Australinea**, or **Meganesia** to distinguish it from the [country of Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia),[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-6)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-7)<sup>[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-8)</sup> is located within the [Southern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Hemisphere) and [Eastern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Hemisphere) hemispheres, near the [Maritime Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_Southeast_Asia).<sup>[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-9)</sup> The continent includes [mainland Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Australia), [Tasmania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tasmania), the island of [New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Guinea) ([Papua New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papua_New_Guinea) and [Western New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_New_Guinea)), the [Aru Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aru_Islands_Regency), the [Ashmore and Cartier Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashmore_and_Cartier_Islands), most of the [Coral Sea Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coral_Sea_Islands), and some other [nearby islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_of_Australia). Situated in the geographical region of [Oceania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceania), more specifically in the subregion of [Australasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australasia), Australia is the [smallest of the seven traditional continents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continent#Area_and_population).

The continent includes a [continental shelf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_shelf) overlain by shallow seas which divide it into several landmasses—the [Arafura Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arafura_Sea) and [Torres Strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torres_Strait) between mainland Australia and New Guinea, and [Bass Strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_Strait) between mainland Australia and Tasmania. When [sea levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level) were lower during the [Pleistocene ice age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternary_glaciation), including the [Last Glacial Maximum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Glacial_Maximum) about 18,000 BC, they were connected by dry land into the combined landmass of [Sahul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahul). The name "Sahul" derives from the [Sahul Shelf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahul_Shelf), which is a part of the continental shelf of the Australian continent. During the past 18,000 to 10,000 years, rising sea levels overflowed the lowlands and separated the continent into today's low-lying [arid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arid) to [semi-arid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-arid_climate) mainland and the two mountainous islands of New Guinea and Tasmania. With a total land area of 8.56 million square kilometres (3,310,000 sq mi), the Australian continent is the smallest, lowest, flattest, and second-driest continent (after [Antarctica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctica)) on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth).<sup>[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-10)</sup> As the country of Australia is mostly on a single landmass, and comprises most of the continent, it is sometimes informally referred to as an island continent, surrounded by oceans.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-11)

Papua New Guinea, a country within the continent, is one of the most [culturally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_diversity) and linguistically diverse countries in the world.<sup>[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Seetharaman-2017-12)</sup> It is also one of the most rural, as only 18 percent of its people live in urban centres.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-13)[West Papua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_New_Guinea), a region in Indonesia, is home to an estimated 44 [uncontacted tribal groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncontacted_peoples).<sup>[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-14)</sup> Australia, the largest landmass in the continent, is highly [urbanised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization),<sup>[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-15)</sup> and has the world's [12th-largest economy](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal)>) with among the highest [human development index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index) globally.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-16)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-17)

The continent of Australia is sometimes known by the names Sahul, Australinea, or Meganesia to differentiate it from the country of Australia, and consists of the landmasses which sit on Australia's continental plate. This includes [mainland Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Australia), [Tasmania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tasmania), and the island of [New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Guinea), which comprises [Papua New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papua_New_Guinea) and [Western New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_New_Guinea) (Papua and West Papua, provinces of [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia)).[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-18)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-19)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-20)<sup>[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-21)</sup> The name "Sahul" takes its name from the [Sahul Shelf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahul_Shelf), which is part of the continental shelf of the Australian continent. The term [Oceania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceania), originally a "great division" of the world in the 1810s, was replaced in [English language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language) countries by the concept of Australia as one of the world's continents in the 1950s.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Lewis-22)

Prior to the 1950s, before the popularisation of the theory of [plate tectonics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_tectonics), [Antarctica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctica), Australia and [Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland) were sometimes described as island continents, but none were usually taught as one of the world's continents in English-speaking countries.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-23)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-24)<sup>[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Lewis-22)</sup> Scottish [cartographer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartographer) [John Bartholomew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bartholomew) wrote in 1873 that, "the [New World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_World) consists of [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America), and the peninsula of [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America) attached to it. These divisions \[are\] generally themselves spoken as continents, and to them has been added another, embracing the large island of Australia and numerous others in the \[Pacific\] Ocean, under the name of Oceania. There are thus six great divisions of the earth—[Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe), [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia), [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa), North America, South America and Oceania."[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-25)

The American author [Samuel Griswold Goodrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Griswold_Goodrich) wrote in his 1854 book *History of All Nations* that, "geographers have agreed to consider the island world of the Pacific Ocean as a third continent, under the name Oceania." In this book the other two continents were categorised as being the New World (consisting of North America and South America) and the [Old World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_World) (consisting of Africa, Asia and Europe).<sup>[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-26)</sup> In his 1879 book *Australasia*, British naturalist [Alfred Russel Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Russel_Wallace) commented that, "Oceania is the word often used by continental geographers to describe the great world of islands we are now entering upon" and that "Australia forms its central and most important feature."<sup>[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Wallace-1879-27)</sup> He did not explicitly label Oceania a continent in the book, but did note that it was one of the six major divisions of the world.<sup>[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Wallace-1879-27)</sup> He considered it to encompass the insular Pacific area between Asia and the Americas, and claimed it extended up to the [Aleutian Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleutian_Islands), which are among the northernmost islands in the Pacific Ocean.<sup>[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Wallace-1879-27)</sup> However, definitions of Oceania varied during the 19th century. In the 19th century, many geographers divided up Oceania into mostly racially-based subdivisions; *[Australasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australasia)*, [*Malaysia* (encompassing *Malay Archipelago*)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malay_Archipelago), *[Melanesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melanesia)*, *[Micronesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micronesia)* and *[Polynesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polynesia)*.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Cornell-1857-28)

Today, the *Malay Archipelago* is typically considered part of [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia), and the term [Oceania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceania) is often used to denote the region encompassing the Australian continent, [Zealandia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zealandia), and [various islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Islands) in the [Pacific Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean) that are not included in the [seven-continent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continent) model. It has been recognised by the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations) as one of the world's five major continental divisions since its foundation in 1947, along with [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa), [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia), [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe) and the [Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americas).[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-29)<sup>[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-30)</sup> The UN's definition of Oceania utilizes four of the five subregions from the 19th century; *Australasia*, *Melanesia*, *Micronesia*, and *Polynesia*. They include [American Samoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Samoa), [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia) and their [external territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/States_and_territories_of_Australia), the [Cook Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook_Islands), [Easter The island states of [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia), [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan), the [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines), [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore) and [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan), all located within the bounds of the Pacific or associated [marginal seas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marginal_sea), are excluded from the UN definition. The states of [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong) and [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia), located in both mainland Asia and marginal seas of the Pacific, are also excluded, as is the nation of [Brunei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunei), which shares the island of [Borneo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borneo) with Indonesia and Malaysia. Further excluded are [East Timor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Timor) and [Indonesian (or Western) New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_New_Guinea), areas which are biogeographically or geologically associated with the Australian landmass.<sup>[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-33)</sup> This definition of Oceania is used in statistical reports, by the [International Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee), and by many atlases.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-34)[The CIA World Factbook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_World_Factbook) also categorise Oceania or the Pacific area as one of the world's major continental divisions, but use the term "Australia and Oceania" to refer to the area.<sup>[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-35)</sup> Their definition does not include Australia's subantarctic external territory [Heard Island and McDonald Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heard_Island_and_McDonald_Islands), but is otherwise the same as the UN definition, and it is also used for statistical purposes.

In countries such as [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina), [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China), [Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile), [Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica), [Ecuador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecuador), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France), [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy), [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico), the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands), [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain), [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland) and [Venezuela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venezuela), Oceania is treated as a continent in the sense that it is "one of the parts of the world", and Australia is only seen as an island nation. In other countries, including [Kazakhstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazakhstan), [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland) and [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia), Australia and [Eurasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasia) are thought of as continents, while Asia, Europe and Oceania are regarded as "parts of the world".<sup>[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-36)</sup> In the *Pacific Ocean Handbook* (1945), author Eliot Grinnell Mears wrote that he categorised Australia, New Zealand and Pacific islands under the label of Oceania for "scientific reasons; Australia's fauna is largely continental in character, New Zealand's are clearly insular; and neither [Commonwealth realm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations) has close ties with Asia." He further added that, "the term *Australasia* is not relished by [New Zealanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealanders) and this name is too often confused with *Australia*."<sup>[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-37)</sup> Some 19th century definitions of Oceania grouped Australia, New Zealand and the islands of Melanesia together under the label of *Australasia*, in other 19th century definitions of Oceania, the term was only used to refer to Australia itself, with New Zealand being categorised with the islands of Polynesia in such definitions.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-38)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Cornell-1857-28)

Archaeological terminology for this region has changed repeatedly. Before the 1970s, the single Pleistocene landmass was called *Australasia*, derived from the [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin) *australis*, meaning "southern", although this word is most often used for a wider region that includes lands like New Zealand that are not on the same continental shelf. In the early 1970s, the term *Greater Australia* was introduced for the Pleistocene continent.<sup>[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Ballard-1993-39)</sup> Then at a 1975 conference and consequent publication,<sup>[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-40)</sup> the name *Sahul* was extended from its previous use for just the [Sahul Shelf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahul_Shelf) to cover the continent.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-Ballard-1993-39)

In 1984, the name *Meganesia* was suggested, meaning "great island" or "great island-group", for both the Pleistocene continent and the present-day lands,<sup>[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-41)</sup> and this name has been widely accepted by biologists.<sup>[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-42)</sup> Others have used *Meganesia* with different meanings: travel writer [Paul Theroux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Theroux) included New Zealand in his definition<sup>[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-43)</sup> and others have used it for Australia, New Zealand and [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii).<sup>[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-44)</sup> Another biologist, [Richard Dawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Dawkins), coined the name *Australinea* in 2004.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-45)*Australia–New Guinea* has also been used.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-46)

The Australian continent and [Sunda](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunda_(landmass)>) were points of early human migrations after leaving Africa.<sup>[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-47)</sup> Research points to a planned migration of hundreds of people using bamboo rafts, which eventually landed on Sahul.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-48)[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-49)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-50)

[Indigenous Australians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_Australians), that is [Aboriginal Australians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aboriginal_Australians) and [Torres Strait Islanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torres_Strait_Islanders) people, are the original inhabitants of the Australian continent and nearby islands. They migrated from Africa to Asia around 70,000 years ago<sup>[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-51)</sup> and arrived in Australia at least 50,000 years ago, based on archaeological evidence.<sup>[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-52)</sup> More recent research points to earlier arrival, possibly 65,000 years ago.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-53)

They are believed to be among the [earliest human migrations out of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recent_African_origin_of_modern_humans). There is evidence of genetic and linguistic interchange between Australians in the far north and the Austronesian peoples of modern-day [New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Guinea) and the islands, but this may be the result of recent trade and [intermarriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interracial_marriage).<sup>[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-54)</sup> The [earliest known human remains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mungo_Man) were found at [Lake Mungo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Mungo_remains), a dry lake in the southwest of New South Wales.<sup>[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-55)</sup> Remains found at Mungo suggest one of the world's oldest known [cremations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cremation), thus indicating early evidence for religious ritual among humans.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-56)[Dreamtime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreamtime) remains a prominent feature of [Australian Aboriginal art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Aboriginal_art), the oldest continuing tradition of art in the world.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-57)

[Papuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papuan_peoples) habitation is estimated to have begun between 42,000 and 48,000 years ago in New Guinea.<sup>[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-58)</sup> Trade between New Guinea and neighboring Indonesian islands was documented as early as the seventh century, and archipelagic rule of New Guinea by the 13th. At the beginning of the seventh century, the [Sumatra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumatra)-based empire of [Srivijaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Srivijaya) (7th century–13th century) engaged in trade relations with western New Guinea, initially taking items like [sandalwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandalwood) and [birds-of-paradise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birds-of-paradise) in [tribute to China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tributaries_of_Imperial_China), but later making slaves out of the natives.<sup>[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-59)</sup> The rule of the [Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java)-based empire of [Majapahit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majapahit) (1293–1527) extended to the western fringes of New Guinea.<sup>[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-60)</sup> Recent archaeological research suggests that 50,000 years ago people may have occupied sites in the highlands at New Guinean altitudes of up to 2,000 m (6,600 ft), rather than being restricted to warmer coastal areas.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-61)

Legends of Terra Australis Incognita—an "unknown land of the South"—date back to Roman times and before, and were commonplace in medieval geography, although not based on any documented knowledge of the continent.<sup>[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-62)</sup> Ancient Greek philosopher [Aristotle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle) speculated of a large landmass in the southern hemisphere, saying, "Now since there must be a region bearing the same relation to the southern pole as the place we live in bears to our pole...".<sup>[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-63)</sup> His ideas were later expanded by [Ptolemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ptolemy) (2nd century AD), who believed that the lands of the [Northern Hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Hemisphere) should be balanced by land in the [south](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Hemisphere). The theory of balancing land has been documented as early as the 5th century on maps by [Macrobius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macrobius), who uses the term Australis on his maps.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-64)

[Terra Australis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terra_Australis), a hypothetical [continent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continent) first posited in [antiquity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_antiquity), appeared on maps between the 15th and 18th centuries.<sup>[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-65)</sup> Scientists, such as [Gerardus Mercator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerardus_Mercator) (1569)<sup>[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-66)</sup> and [Alexander Dalrymple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Dalrymple) as late as 1767 argued for its existence, with such arguments as that there should be a large [landmass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landmass) in the [south](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Hemisphere) as a [counterweight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterweight) to the known landmasses in the Northern Hemisphere.<sup>[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-67)</sup> The cartographic depictions of the southern continent in the 16th and early 17th centuries, as might be expected for a concept based on such abundant conjecture and minimal data, varied wildly from map to map; in general, the continent shrank as potential locations were reinterpreted. At its largest, the continent included [Tierra del Fuego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tierra_del_Fuego), separated from South America by a small strait; [New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Guinea); and what would come to be called Australia.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-68)

In 1606, Dutch navigator [Willem Janszoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willem_Janszoon) made the first documented European sight and landing on the continent of Australia in [Cape York Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_York_Peninsula).<sup>[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-69)</sup> Dutch explorer [Abel Janszoon Tasman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel_Tasman) circumnavigated and landed on parts of the [Australian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia) continental coast and discovered [Van Diemen's Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Diemen's_Land) (now [Tasmania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tasmania)), [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand) in 1642, and [Fiji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiji) islands.<sup>[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-70)</sup> He was the first known European explorer to reach these islands.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-71)

In the quest for [Terra Australis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terra_Australis), Spanish explorations in the 17th century, such as the expedition led by the Portuguese navigator [Pedro Fernandes de Queirós](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Fernandes_de_Queirós), discovered the [Pitcairn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitcairn_Islands) and [Vanuatu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanuatu) archipelagos, and sailed the [Torres Strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torres_Strait) between [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia) and [New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Guinea), named after navigator [Luís Vaz de Torres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luís_Vaz_de_Torres), who was the first European to explore the Strait. When [Europeans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe) first arrived, inhabitants of New Guinea and nearby islands, whose technologies included bone, wood, and stone tools, had a productive agricultural system. In 1660, the Dutch recognised the Sultan of [Tidore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tidore)'s sovereignty over [New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Guinea). The first known Europeans to sight New Guinea were probably the [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_people) and [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_people) navigators sailing in the South Pacific in the early part of the 16th century.

On 23 April 1770, British explorer [James Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cook) made his first recorded direct observation of [indigenous Australians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_Australians) at [Brush Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brush_Island) near [Bawley Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bawley_Point,_New_South_Wales).<sup>[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-72)</sup> On 29 April, Cook and crew made their first landfall on the mainland of the continent at a place now known as the [Kurnell Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cronulla_sand_dunes,_Kurnell_Peninsula). It is here that James Cook made first contact with an Aboriginal tribe known as the [Gweagal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gweagal), who he fired upon, injuring one.<sup>[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-73)</sup> His expedition became the first recorded Europeans to have encountered the eastern coastline of Australia.<sup>[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-74)</sup> Captain [Arthur Phillip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Phillip) led the *[First Fleet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Fleet)* of 11 ships and about 850 convicts into [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney) on 26 January 1788.<sup>[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-75)</sup> This was to be the location for the new colony. Phillip described [Sydney Cove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Cove) as being "without exception the finest harbour in the world".[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-76)

In 1883, the [Colony of Queensland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensland) tried to annex the southern half of eastern New Guinea, but the British government did not approve.<sup>[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-77)</sup> The [Commonwealth of Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Australia) came into being when the [Federal Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Australia) was proclaimed by the [Governor-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor-General_of_Australia), [Lord Hopetoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hope,_1st_Marquess_of_Linlithgow), on 1 January 1901. From that point a system of [federalism in Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federalism_in_Australia) came into operation, entailing the establishment of an entirely new national government (the Commonwealth government) and an ongoing division of powers between that government and the States. With the encouragement of Queensland, in 1884, a [British protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_protectorate) had been proclaimed over the southern coast of New Guinea and its adjacent islands. [British New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_New_Guinea) was annexed outright in 1888. The possession was placed under the authority of the newly federated Commonwealth of Australia in 1902 and with passage of the Papua Act 1905, British New Guinea became the Australian [Territory of Papua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territory_of_Papua), with formal Australian administration beginning in 1906.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-78)

The [Bombing of Darwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombing_of_Darwin) on 19 February 1942 was the largest single attack ever mounted by a foreign power on Australia.<sup>[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-79)</sup> In an effort to isolate Australia, the Japanese planned a seaborne invasion of [Port Moresby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Moresby), in the Australian [Territory of New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territory_of_New_Guinea). Between July and November 1942, Australian forces repulsed Japanese attempts on the city by way of the [Kokoda Track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kokoda_Track_campaign), in the highlands of [New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Guinea). The [Battle of Buna–Gona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Buna–Gona), between November 1942 and January 1943, set the tone for the bitter final stages of the [New Guinea campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Guinea_campaign), which persisted into 1945. The offensives in Papua and New Guinea of 1943–44 were the single largest series of connected operations ever mounted by the Australian armed forces.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-80)

Following the 1998 commencement of [reforms across Indonesia](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformation_(Indonesia)>), Papua and other Indonesian provinces received greater regional autonomy. In 2001, "Special Autonomy" status was granted to Papua province, although to date, implementation has been partial and often criticised.<sup>[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-81)</sup> The region was administered as a single province until 2003, when it was split into the provinces of [Papua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papua,_Indonesia) and [West Papua](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Papua_(province)>). Elections in 1972 resulted in the formation of a ministry headed by Chief Minister [Michael Somare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Somare), who pledged to lead the country to self-government and then to independence. Papua New Guinea became self-governing on 1 December 1973 and achieved independence on 16 September 1975. The country joined the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations) (UN) on 10 October 1975.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-82)

Migration brought large numbers of southern and central Europeans to Australia for the first time. A 1958 government leaflet assured readers that unskilled non-British migrants were needed for "labour on rugged projects ...work which is not generally acceptable to Australians or British workers".<sup>[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-83)</sup> Australia fought on the side of Britain in the two [world wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_war) and became a long-standing [ally of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANZUS) when threatened by [Imperial Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Japan) during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II). Trade with Asia increased and a post-war immigration program received more than 6.5 million migrants from every continent. Supported by immigration of people from more than 200 countries since the end of World War II, the population increased to more than 23 million by 2014.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-84)

The Australian continent, as a whole being part of the [Australian Plate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Plate), is the lowest, flattest, and oldest landmass on Earth<sup>[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-85)</sup> and it has had a relatively stable geological history. [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand) is not part of the continent of Australia, but of the separate, submerged continent of [Zealandia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zealandia).<sup>[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-86)</sup> New Zealand and Australia are both part of the Oceanian sub-region known as [Australasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australasia), with New Guinea being in [Melanesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melanesia).

The continent includes a continental shelf overlain by shallow seas which divide it into several landmasses—the [Arafura Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arafura_Sea) and [Torres Strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torres_Strait) between mainland Australia and New Guinea, and [Bass Strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_Strait) between mainland Australia and Tasmania. When [sea levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level) were lower during the [Pleistocene ice age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternary_glaciation), including the [Last Glacial Maximum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Glacial_Maximum) about 18,000 BC, they were connected by dry land.

During the past 18,000<sup>[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-87)</sup> to 10,000 years, rising sea levels overflowed the lowlands and separated the continent into today's low-lying [arid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arid) to [semi-arid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-arid_climate) mainland and the two mountainous islands of New Guinea and Tasmania.<sup>[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-88)</sup> The [continental shelf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_shelf) connecting the islands, half of which is less than 50 metres (160 ft) deep, covers some 2.5 million square kilometres (970,000 sq mi), including the [Sahul Shelf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahul_Shelf)[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-89)<sup>[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-90)</sup> and [Bass Strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_Strait).

Geological forces such as [tectonic uplift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tectonic_uplift) of mountain ranges or clashes between tectonic plates occurred mainly in Australia's early history, when it was still a part of [Gondwana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gondwana). Australia is situated in the middle of the tectonic plate, and therefore currently has no active volcanism.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-91)

The continent primarily sits on the Indo-Australian Plate. Because of its central location on its tectonic plate, Australia does not have any active volcanic regions, the only continent with this distinction.<sup>[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-92)</sup> The lands were joined with [Antarctica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctica) as part of the southern supercontinent [Gondwana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gondwana) until the plate began to drift north about 96 million years ago.

For most of the time since then, Australia–New Guinea remained a continuous landmass. When the [last glacial period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_glacial_period) ended in about 10,000 BC, rising sea levels formed [Bass Strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_Strait), separating Tasmania from the mainland. Then between about 8,000 and 6,500 BC, the lowlands in the north were flooded by the sea, separating the [Aru Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aru_Islands_Regency), mainland Australia, [New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Guinea), and Tasmania.

A northern arc consisting of the [New Guinea Highlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Guinea_Highlands), the [Raja Ampat Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ampat_Islands), and [Halmahera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halmahera) was uplifted by the northward migration of Australia and subduction of the [Pacific Plate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Plate). The [Outer Banda Arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_Banda_Arc) was accreted along the northwestern edge the continent; it includes the islands of [Timor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timor), [Tanimbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanimbar), and [Seram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seram_Island). Papua New Guinea has [several volcanoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_volcanoes_in_Papua_New_Guinea), as it is situated along the [Pacific Ring of Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ring_of_Fire). Volcanic eruptions are not rare, and the area is prone to [earthquakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthquake) and [tsunamis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsunami) because of this.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-93)[Mount Wilhelm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Wilhelm) in Papua New Guinea is the second highest mountain in the continent,<sup>[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-94)</sup> and at 4,884 metres (16,024 ft) [above sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Above_sea_level), [Puncak Jaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puncak_Jaya) is the [highest mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highest_mountain).

For about 40 million years Australia–New Guinea was almost completely isolated. During this time, the continent experienced numerous changes in climate, but the overall trend was towards greater aridity. When [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America) eventually separated from Antarctica, the development of the cold [Antarctic Circumpolar Current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_Circumpolar_Current) changed weather patterns across the world. For Australia–New Guinea, it brought a marked intensification of the drying trend. The great inland seas and lakes dried out. Much of the long-established broad-leaf [deciduous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deciduous) forest began to give way to the distinctive hard-leaved [sclerophyllous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sclerophyllous) plants that characterise the modern Australian landscape.

Typical Southern Hemisphere flora include the [conifers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conifer) *[Podocarpus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podocarpus)* (eastern Australia and New Guinea), the rainforest emergents *[Araucaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Araucaria)* (eastern Australia and New Guinea), *[Nothofagus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nothofagus)* (New Guinea and [Tasmania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tasmania)) and *[Agathis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agathis)* (northern [Queensland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensland) and New Guinea), as well as [tree ferns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_fern) and several species of *Eucalyptus*. Prominent features of the Australian flora are adaptations to [aridity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aridity) and fire which include [scleromorphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sclerophyll) and [serotiny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serotiny). These adaptations are common in species from the large and well-known families [Proteaceae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proteaceae) (*[Banksias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banksia)* and *[Grevilleas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grevillea)*), [Myrtaceae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myrtaceae) (*[Eucalyptus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eucalyptus)* or gum trees, *[Melaleucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melaleuca)* and *[Callistemons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callistemon)*), [Fabaceae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabaceae) (*[Acacia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acacia)*s or wattles), and [Casuarinaceae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casuarinaceae) (*[Casuarinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casuarina)* or she-oaks), which are typically found in the Australian mainland. The flora of New Guinea is a mixture of many [tropical rainforest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_rainforest) species with origins in Asia, such as [Castanopsis acuminatissima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castanopsis_acuminatissima),*[Lithocarpus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithocarpus)* spp., [elaeocarps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elaeocarpaceae), and [laurels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauraceae), together with typically Australasian flora. In the New Guinean highlands, conifers such as *[Dacrycarpus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dacrycarpus), [Dacrydium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dacrydium), [Papuacedrus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papuacedrus)* and *[Libocedrus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libocedrus)* are present.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-95)

For many species, the primary refuge was the relatively cool and well-watered [Great Dividing Range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Dividing_Range). Even today, pockets of remnant vegetation remain in the cool uplands, some species not much changed from the Gondwanan forms of 60 or 90 million years ago. Eventually, the Australia–New Guinea tectonic plate collided with the [Eurasian plate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasian_plate) to the north. The collision caused the northern part of the continent to buckle upwards, forming the high and rugged mountains of New Guinea and, by reverse (downwards) buckling, the [Torres Strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torres_Strait) that now separates the two main landmasses. The collision also pushed up the islands of [Wallacea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallacea), which served as island 'stepping-stones' that allowed plants from [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia)'s rainforests to colonise New Guinea, and some plants from Australia–New Guinea to move into Southeast Asia. The ocean straits between the islands were narrow enough to allow plant dispersal, but served as an effective barrier to exchange of land mammals between Australia–New Guinea and Asia. Among the fungi, the remarkable association between [Cyttaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyttaria)*gunnii* (one of the "golf-ball" fungi) and its associated trees in the genus *[Nothofagus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nothofagus)* is evidence of that drift: the only other places where this association is known are New Zealand and southern [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina) and [Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile).[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-96)

Due to the spread of animals, fungi and plants across the single Pleistocene landmass the separate lands have a related [biota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biome).<sup>[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-97)</sup> There are over 300 bird species in [West Papua](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Papua_(province)>), of which at least 20 are unique to the ecoregion, and some live only in very restricted areas. These include the [grey-banded munia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey-banded_munia), [Vogelkop bowerbird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vogelkop_bowerbird), and the [king bird-of-paradise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_bird-of-paradise).[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-98)

Australia has a huge variety of animals; some 83% of [mammals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammals_of_Australia), 89% of [reptiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reptiles_of_Australia), 24% of fish and insects and 93% of [amphibians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphibian) that inhabit the continent are [endemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endemic) to Australia.<sup>[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org#cite_note-99)</sup> This high level of endemism can be attributed to the continent's long geographic isolation, [tectonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_tectonics) stability, and the effects of an unusual pattern of climate change on the soil and [flora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flora_of_Australia) over geological time.
